video_title: Rational Security: “The Right Kind of American for Rational Security” Edition
gist: Lawfare's Scott R. Anderson, Julia Curley and Natalie Orpett assess the September 2026 Xi Jinping state visit to Washington (expected outcome: an extension of the US-China tariff and rare-earth truce expiring November 10, with Taiwan's $14B arms package and AI coordination as risks), the US-Denmark-Greenland security agreement (largely a modest update of the 1951 treaty plus bars on non-NATO bases and sensitive foreign investment), and reported US plans to sanction the International Criminal Court as an institution, which the panel warns could trigger an EU blocking statute and accelerate de-dollarization among allies.

themes.theme: Xi-Trump summit: tariff and rare-earth truce

insights.claim: The US-China 90-day tariff truce expires November 10, 2026, and the most likely outcome of Xi Jinping's September 2026 Washington state visit is an extension of the trade and rare-earth truce past the US midterm elections into 2027, rather than a substantive breakthrough.
insights.speaker: Julia Curley
insights.so_what: Base case is continuation of the 'managed stalemate'; tariff-cliff tail risk around Nov 10 is likely defused, supporting China-exposed equities and supply chains near term.
insights.quote: If they get their way, if the White House manages, we'll have an extension of the trade and rare earth truce, past the elections, passed into next year

insights.claim: Beijing wants a tariff-war abatement lasting until the end of Trump's term, but Trump prefers short extensions to preserve leverage, so trade truces are likely to keep rolling on short (roughly six-month) cycles tied to summits.
insights.speaker: Julia Curley
insights.so_what: Expect recurring truce-expiry deadlines as volatility catalysts rather than a durable settlement; price US-China trade risk as periodically renewed, not resolved.
insights.quote: Beijing would like a much longer agreement. They would prefer to have an abatement of the the tariff competition or the the tariff war until after Trump's term. But Trump wanting to have continued leverage is unlikely to get it.

insights.claim: Trump's concrete trade asks of Xi are narrow: continued announcements of Chinese soybean purchases and relief from pressure on US companies such as Boeing that face higher costs in China.
insights.speaker: Julia Curley
insights.so_what: Soybean purchase announcements and Boeing China relief are the likeliest tangible summit deliverables to watch for BA and ag commodities.
insights.quote: He really just wants continued announcements of soybean sales and maybe an abatement of some of the pressure on US companies like Boeing who face higher costs in in China

insights.claim: China's threat of rare-earth mineral export controls is a major stick hanging over trade talks, and because the Trump administration sees AI as a key driver of the US economy it avoids confronting Beijing on trade, which has pushed US posture toward accommodation.
insights.speaker: Scott R. Anderson
insights.so_what: Rare-earth leverage effectively caps US trade escalation; AI/semiconductor supply-chain dependence on Chinese rare earths is a structural constraint on US policy.

insights.claim: US posture toward China has shifted from the first Trump term's and Biden's great-power-rivalry framing to an effort at accommodation; the Trump national security strategy expressly accepts China (and to a lesser extent Russia) having spheres of influence.
insights.speaker: Scott R. Anderson
insights.so_what: A spheres-of-influence doctrine lowers the odds of US escalation against China but raises regional security risk for allies like Taiwan, Japan and Europe.

insights.claim: US China policy is ad hoc with whiplash messaging from issue to issue; no one in the administration appears to be managing the full set of US-China issues or trading one against another, and Congressional China hawks only speak up when given permission by administration messaging.
insights.speaker: Natalie Orpett
insights.so_what: Headline risk around China policy is driven by presidential improvisation rather than process; Congress is not a reliable check on concessions.

insights.claim: China nixed at the last minute a plan to bring a delegation of senior corporate executives, weighted toward AI, to the Washington summit, possibly to keep state control over its tech industry and limit direct industry-to-industry contacts.
insights.speaker: Scott R. Anderson
insights.so_what: Signals Beijing is tightening control over private-sector engagement with the US; don't expect summit-driven commercial deals for Chinese tech firms.

themes.theme: Taiwan arms sale as bargaining chip

insights.claim: Trump has suspended a roughly $14 billion Taiwan arms package of air-defense systems (Patriot and NASAMS) and said he wants to use it as a bargaining chip with Beijing, which the panel says contradicts the Taiwan Relations Act.
insights.speaker: Julia Curley
insights.so_what: A large foreign military sale for air-defense makers (Patriot/NASAMS supply chain) is held up and could be permanently shelved in a US-China deal; watch summit statements.
insights.quote: the president has held up what is one of the largest arm sales in history to Taiwan of defensive air defense systems

insights.claim: The biggest risk from the Xi-Trump summit is unscripted presidential remarks on Taiwan that signal Taipei cannot count on US support, since most of the summit is informal and no follow-on technical negotiations are planned.
insights.speaker: Julia Curley
insights.so_what: Headline risk for Taiwan equities and semiconductor supply-chain risk premia hinges on off-script comments rather than formal agreements.
insights.quote: the remarks the president makes are likely to be the most consequential things that that come out of it

insights.claim: Trump has said he does not see the point of the US going 9,000 miles to defend Taiwan, though his administration values Taiwan's semiconductor production and has spoken of deterring conflict.
insights.speaker: Julia Curley
insights.so_what: Weakened US deterrence raises the tail risk around Taiwan semiconductor supply that markets may underprice.

insights.claim: Munitions spent in the Iran war, especially air defense, and overuse of aircraft carriers have directly reduced US ability to surge forces to East Asia for a Taiwan contingency.
insights.speaker: Julia Curley
insights.so_what: Depleted air-defense and munitions stockpiles imply sustained replenishment demand for defense primes and weaker Indo-Pacific deterrence.
insights.quote: the number of munitions expended in the Iran war has come directly at the expense of the ability of the US to surge forces, especially air defense to the region in East Asia

insights.claim: Xi wants Trump to commit to attending an APEC summit in November where he would stand alongside Xi and Putin, which the panel frames as a risky Yalta-style image of great-power spheres.
insights.speaker: Julia Curley
insights.so_what: A November APEC trilateral photo-op would be a further signal of spheres-of-influence diplomacy with implications for allies' security spending.

insights.claim: Leaders of major AI companies, including Elon Musk, Anthropic's Dario Amodei, OpenAI and Google, are now calling for a framework to share information on frontier models and safety testing, shifting US political momentum toward AI regulation even as Trump dismisses it.
insights.speaker: Scott R. Anderson
insights.so_what: Industry-led AI regulation is gaining momentum; regulatory risk for frontier labs may come from self-imposed frameworks rather than Washington.

insights.claim: US-China AI talks are unlikely to go beyond an exchange of contact details at cabinet level (e.g., Treasury Secretary Bessent), with no planned technical working-level follow-up on containment of rogue AI agents.
insights.speaker: Julia Curley
insights.so_what: No substantive US-China AI governance is coming soon; the AI race framing and export controls persist.
insights.quote: that agreement does not seem to go any further than just the exchange of of phone numbers

insights.claim: As with nuclear arms control, China has little incentive to enter deep AI talks until it reaches rough parity, because it sees US GPU and compute export restrictions as an effort to hold back its AI development.
insights.speaker: Julia Curley
insights.so_what: Expect continued chip export controls and a compute race; Chinese domestic AI and semiconductor build-out stays a strategic priority.

insights.claim: China already regulates its AI industry more heavily than the US, so the idea of a government role in AI development is far less contested in Beijing than in Washington.
insights.speaker: Natalie Orpett
insights.so_what: Different regulatory baselines limit how far bilateral AI governance talks can progress.

insights.claim: The Trump administration has a track record of bringing US executives together with foreign officials to facilitate business deals, and AI company heads are attending the state dinner for Xi, where commercial access to the China market may be on the table.
insights.speaker: Natalie Orpett
insights.so_what: Watch for company-specific China deal announcements around the state visit.

insights.claim: Trump announced the creation of an 'AI force', a new US military branch, and rebranded AI as 'superintelligence'.
insights.speaker: Julia Curley
insights.so_what: A dedicated military AI branch implies new defense AI budget lines, a potential tailwind for defense-tech and AI contractors.
insights.quote: the president this week announced that we will be forming an AI force

themes.theme: Iran war and China's energy resilience

insights.claim: China, Iran's key oil lifeline, built significant oil and gas stockpiles before the Iran war and came through the energy disruption stronger than many US allies by buying less on international markets.
insights.speaker: Julia Curley
insights.so_what: Chinese stockpiling dampened its import demand during the shock; China is not a forced buyer and has leverage over energy-hungry neighbors.
insights.quote: they had built up a significant stockpile of oil and gas to get through the the disruption

insights.claim: Other countries have felt the Iran war's global energy shock far more heavily than the US or China, and the US is being blamed for price spikes and inflation while China is seen as a responsible actor.
insights.speaker: Scott R. Anderson
insights.so_what: Energy-importing economies (Europe, Asia ex-China) bear the brunt of the shock; the reputational shift favors Chinese diplomatic leverage.

insights.claim: China has not complied with US secondary sanctions on Iran and is unlikely to publicly back the US on ending the Iran war at the summit.
insights.speaker: Julia Curley
insights.so_what: Chinese purchases of Iranian oil will continue to blunt US sanctions; don't expect a US-China-brokered Iran resolution.

insights.claim: At the UN General Assembly Trump threatened to annihilate Iran while senior administration officials simultaneously met Iranian officials in New York about a potential deal, with no visible progress so far.
insights.speaker: Scott R. Anderson
insights.so_what: Back-channel Iran talks are an upside catalyst for oil if they progress; the public rhetoric is a poor guide.

insights.claim: In his UN speech Trump claimed 'to the victor go the spoils' of Venezuela's oil economy, signaling a might-makes-right posture on resource control.
insights.speaker: Julia Curley
insights.so_what: US control over Venezuelan oil is openly framed as a spoil of intervention; relevant to Venezuelan supply and energy-company access.
insights.quote: He also talked about Venezuela and and loudly proclaiming that to the victor go the spoils of of the Venezuelan oil economy

insights.claim: A US-Denmark-Greenland agreement bars non-NATO military presence in Greenland and restricts investment in sensitive sectors by non-EU/non-NATO countries (aimed at China and Russia), pointing to new foreign-investment screening frameworks there.
insights.speaker: Scott R. Anderson
insights.so_what: Chinese capital is effectively locked out of Greenland's minerals and infrastructure; Western-aligned investors gain relative access.

insights.claim: The Greenland agreement adds little to the 1951 US-Denmark defense treaty beyond language on China and mineral rights that Denmark had offered before the 18-month US coercion campaign, which badly damaged relations with one of Europe's most pro-American allies.
insights.speaker: Julia Curley
insights.so_what: Trump's 'permanent control' framing overstates the deal; the lasting effect is eroded European trust in the US.
insights.quote: we basically got just slight updates on what we already had for the low low price of almost destroying our relationship with one of the most pro-American countries in Europe

insights.claim: The Greenland deal requires Danish and Greenlandic parliamentary approval with no scheduled votes, and Denmark and Greenland are expected to slow-walk ratification and new consultative bodies to keep the issue on the back burner until 2029.
insights.speaker: Scott R. Anderson
insights.so_what: Expect slow implementation of new US bases or investment rules; renewed US base demands could reignite the dispute.

insights.claim: The Greenland crisis was the most dramatic psychological break for Europe in its relations with the US in the postwar era, and the new agreement is unlikely to repair that because the reaction reached European domestic politics.
insights.speaker: Natalie Orpett
insights.so_what: Lasting transatlantic distrust supports European strategic-autonomy moves (defense spending, financial independence from the US).

insights.claim: Trump's pattern is to escalate absurd, exploitative rhetoric before a deal so the final terms look reasonable by comparison, as with the Ukraine minerals deal and now Greenland.
insights.speaker: Natalie Orpett
insights.so_what: Discount maximalist opening threats; final Trump deals tend to converge toward existing arrangements.

insights.claim: The Trump administration has reportedly drafted sanctions targeting the International Criminal Court as an institution, not just individual judges and prosecutors, which could cut the court and anyone supporting it off from the global financial system.
insights.speaker: Scott R. Anderson
insights.so_what: Entity-level ICC sanctions would create compliance exposure for European banks, contractors and governments dealing with the court.

insights.claim: If the US imposes institution-wide ICC sanctions, the EU could activate its rarely used blocking statute, prohibiting EU entities from complying with extraterritorial US sanctions.
insights.speaker: Natalie Orpett
insights.so_what: A blocking statute would put European banks in a legal bind between US and EU law, a compliance and legal-risk flashpoint.

insights.claim: Fully enforcing ICC sanctions by cutting off allied governments and foreign banks with US correspondent accounts would be a major driver of de-dollarization among the European allies and market economies most essential to dollar hegemony, on top of Greenland and Iran.
insights.speaker: Scott R. Anderson
insights.so_what: Weaponizing dollar access against allies is a long-term risk to dollar reserve status; watch for European payment-system and reserve diversification.
insights.quote: If you want to know what could drive deolarization among the audiences that are most essential to maintaining the hegemony of the dollar

insights.claim: The likeliest outcome on the ICC is a broadly worded executive order that allows wide designations but is applied lightly and strategically, because full enforcement would trigger a Greenland-style crisis with allies.
insights.speaker: Scott R. Anderson
insights.so_what: Headline risk is likely bigger than the eventual enforcement; the key signal is the number of actual designations.

insights.claim: Past ICC-related sanctions affecting US nationals have been enjoined by federal courts on First Amendment and Berman Amendment (IEEPA informational-materials exemption) grounds, so new ICC sanctions reportedly avoid regulating communicative materials and focus on foreign actors.
insights.speaker: Scott R. Anderson
insights.so_what: US sanctions design is shifting toward foreign targets to avoid domestic litigation, increasing the burden on non-US institutions.

insights.claim: The US has given about $3.8 billion in humanitarian assistance to the UN in recent years, partly because dismantling USAID makes direct delivery harder, showing the administration still relies on UN mechanisms despite its rhetoric.
insights.speaker: Scott R. Anderson
insights.so_what: Anti-UN rhetoric overstates actual policy change; funding flows through multilateral channels continue.
